question: Directive 89/391/EEC requires employers to ensure the health and safety of workers in all aspects of their work and, in particular, sets out obligations regarding the prevention of occupational risks.

In addition, Article 5 of Directive 2000/78/EC provides that employers shall, where necessary, take appropriate measures to ensure reasonable accommodation for people with disabilities, except where this would constitute a disproportionate burden.

However, certain situations may lead the same worker to perform several functions in the context of different employment relationships or statuses, involving different employers or competent authorities. 1.
To what extent do the obligations arising from Directives 89/391/EEC and 2000/78/EC apply in such situations?
Does EU law impose specific obligations on the various employers or authorities concerned to coordinate their actions in order to ensure that these protections are effective?
In the absence of such obligations, is it up to the Member States to determine the coordination arrangements and the allocation of responsibilities between the various actors involved?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the author: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.11.2026) Directive 89/391/EEC1 requires each employer to ensure the occupational safety and health (OSH) of workers in all work-related aspects. Within their responsibilities, employers must assess OSH risks, take into consideration the workers’ capabilities as regards OSH, and take the necessary preventive and protective measures.

Directive 2000/78/EC2 requires individual employers to provide reasonable accommodation where needed in a particular case, unless this imposes a disproportionate burden. No EU OSH directive requires coordination between employers or authorities where a worker has multiple employers or employment relationships.

Article 6(4) of Directive 89/391/EEC requires employers sharing a workplace to cooperate in implementing safety, health and occupational hygiene provisions3, to coordinate OSH actions, and to inform each other and workers and/or their representatives of the risks. Directive 2000/78/EC likewise requires no coordination between employers or authorities in case of multiple employers of the same worker.

EU OSH directives set minimum requirements allowing Member States to adopt more stringent and detailed provisions for the protection of workers. They may also introduce or maintain provisions more favourable to equal treatment than those required by Directive 2000/78/EC.

Regarding working conditions, in its Communication Enhancing the Strategy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities up to 20304, the Commission states that it will seek to consider OSH risks faced by workers with disabilities in the envisaged Quality Jobs Act proposal, following the relevant social partners' consultation.
1 Council Directive 89/391/EEC of 12 June 1989 on the introduction of measures to encourage improvements in

the safety and health of workers at work, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/1989/391/2008-12-11. 2 Council Directive 2000/78/EC of 27 November 2000 establishing a general framework for equal treatment in employment and occupation, OJ L 303, 2.12.2000, pp. 16–22, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2000/78/oj/eng.

3 All provisions of Council Directive 89/391/EEC and the provisions of the related directives within the meaning of Article 16 (1) of Directive 89/391/EEC. 4 https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/ab0bcea9-6b3a-48c1-875c1cc687fba6d0_en?filename=EC%20Enhancing%20the%20disability%20strategy%20up%20to%202030.pdf.
